question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
One that cannot be harmed/wounded
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Invulnerable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Invulnerable" means incapable of being harmed, injured, or wounded; something that cannot be damaged or defeated. (जिसे चोट न पहुंचाई जा सके / अजेय)
◦ Example: The old fort was believed to be invulnerable to any attack.

• The word is formed by adding the negative prefix "in-" to "vulnerable" (capable of being hurt), giving the opposite meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Mortal (नश्वर): Subject to death; liable to die — the opposite of immortal, and unrelated to being harmed.

• Option 2: Mystic (रहस्यमय): A person who seeks spiritual truth through contemplation, or something mysterious/spiritual in nature.

• Option 4: Bigot (कट्टरपंथी): A person who is intolerant of opinions, beliefs, or people that differ from their own.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutions with the prefix "in-/im-": Impeccable (without fault), Incorrigible (incapable of being corrected), Immutable (unchangeable).

• Related words: Invincible (that cannot be defeated), Invaluable (too precious to be valued).

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: Your employes also have acess to this data.
option_2: Your employes also have access to this data.
option_3: Your employees also have acces to this datas.
option_4: Your employees also have access to this data.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Your employees also have access to this data.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correctly spelt sentence uses "employees" (the plural of "employee", formed with the suffix "-ee" + "-s") and "access" (meaning the means or right to obtain or make use of something), spelt with a double "c" and a single "s".

• Spelling key: EMPLOY + EE + S → employees; AC + CESS → access (not "acess" or "acces").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Your employes also have acess to this data." — incorrect; "employes" is missing an "e" (should be "employees") and "acess" is missing a "c" (should be "access").

• Option 2: "Your employes also have access to this data." — incorrect; "employes" is misspelt, missing an "e" (should be "employees"), although "access" is correctly spelt here.

• Option 3: "Your employees also have acces to this datas." — incorrect; "acces" is missing an "s" (should be "access") and "datas" wrongly adds a plural "-s" to "data", which does not take one in standard usage.

NOTE

• "Data" is traditionally treated as the plural of "datum" and is generally used without an additional "-s"; in modern usage it is also accepted as an uncountable noun (e.g., "the data is/are correct").

• Other frequently confused spellings in SSC exams: Occurrence, Accommodate, Necessary, Embarrass, Millennium, Questionnaire — each has a doubled letter that test-takers commonly miss.

question:
The given sentence is in active voice. Change the voice of the sentence. Select the correct option from the sentences given in options.
She persuaded him for over a year.
option_1: He was being persuaded by her for a year.
option_2: He kept being persuaded by her for a year.
option_3: He was persuaded by her for over a year.
option_4: She was being persuaded by him for over a year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. He was persuaded by her for over a year.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "She persuaded him for over a year" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "him" becomes the subject "he"; since the subject is singular, the auxiliary used is "was"; the verb "persuaded" (V2) becomes the past participle "persuaded" (V3, as it is a regular verb); and "she" becomes the agent "her" with "by". The time expression "for over a year" is retained unchanged.
◦ Passive: He was persuaded by her for over a year.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it drops the word "over" — it reads "for a year" instead of "for over a year", changing the meaning of the original sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "kept being persuaded" wrongly suggests a repeated or continuous passive action, which changes the sense of the original simple past sentence and is not the standard passive form.

• Option 4 is incorrect because the subject and object have been interchanged wrongly ("She was being persuaded by him"), which reverses who is persuading whom, and it also wrongly uses the continuous passive form "was being persuaded" instead of the simple past passive.

NOTE

• Time expressions and adverbials (like "for over a year", "yesterday", "last week") must always be carried over unchanged from the active sentence to the passive sentence.

• Do not confuse the Simple Past Passive (was/were + V3) with the Past Continuous Passive (was/were + being + V3); the latter is used for an action that was ongoing at a specific past moment, not for a completed simple past action.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. requires knowledge of the complex interplay among ocean
Q. chemistry and circulation, ecology of marine and terrestrial
R. organisms, ice sheet dynamics, and atmospheric chemistry and circulation
S. a full understanding of glacial-interglacial carbon dynamics
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. SPQR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In sentence-rearrangement (para jumble) questions, look for the part that can stand as a complete opening idea (usually containing the main subject) and then trace the logical chain through pronouns, conjunctions and continuing phrases.

• Part S — "a full understanding of glacial-interglacial carbon dynamics" — introduces the subject of the sentence and logically comes first.

• Part P — "requires knowledge of the complex interplay among ocean" — supplies the verb "requires" for the subject in S, and its final word "ocean" needs a continuation, so it must be followed by Q.

• Part Q — "chemistry and circulation, ecology of marine and terrestrial" — continues the list started by "ocean" (ocean chemistry and circulation) and begins a second list (ecology of marine and terrestrial ...), which is completed by R.

• Part R — "organisms, ice sheet dynamics, and atmospheric chemistry and circulation" — completes "marine and terrestrial organisms" and finishes the sentence.

• Reading S-P-Q-R together: "A full understanding of glacial-interglacial carbon dynamics requires knowledge of the complex interplay among ocean chemistry and circulation, ecology of marine and terrestrial organisms, ice sheet dynamics, and atmospheric chemistry and circulation." This forms a complete, logically connected sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PQRS) is incorrect because it begins with "requires knowledge...", which has no subject to attach to — a sentence cannot logically begin with "requires".

• Option 2 (QPRS) is incorrect because it begins with part Q, which starts mid-list ("chemistry and circulation...") and has no antecedent for what these are the chemistry/circulation of.

• Option 4 (SRPQ) is incorrect because after S, part R ("organisms, ice sheet dynamics...") does not logically follow — "organisms" needs the earlier phrase "marine and terrestrial" (from Q) to make sense, and P's "requires knowledge... among ocean" would be left dangling before Q.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always locate the part with the main subject and verb first (here S+P), then use linking words, lists, and grammatical continuations (ocean → chemistry and circulation; terrestrial → organisms) to fix the remaining order.

• Reading the fully joined sentence back to check that it makes complete logical and grammatical sense is the most reliable final check.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
They hired a maid to have cleaner the house.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. to clean.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "They hired a maid to have cleaner the house" uses the infinitive of purpose, which requires the base form of the verb after "to".

• Rule — Infinitive of Purpose: When "to + verb" is used to express the purpose of an action (why something is done), the verb must be in its base form (V1): Subject + Verb + Object + to + V1 + Object.

• Applying the rule: "hired a maid to clean the house" correctly uses the base verb "clean" after "to", expressing the purpose for which the maid was hired.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "to cleans" is incorrect because the infinitive "to" must always be followed by the base form of the verb, never a form with "-s" (which is used only for third person singular in the present tense).

• Option 2: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original phrase "to have cleaner the house" is ungrammatical — "cleaner" is a comparative adjective/noun here, not a verb, and cannot follow "to have" in this construction; the sentence does need improvement.

• Option 4: "for cleaner" is incorrect because "for" changes the construction to a prepositional phrase and "cleaner" remains a non-verb form, which does not correctly express the purpose of hiring the maid.

NOTE

• Common infinitive-of-purpose errors tested by SSC: using "for + V-ing" instead of "to + V1" (e.g., "He went to market for buying vegetables" should be "to buy vegetables").

• Do not confuse "to clean" (infinitive, purpose) with "cleaning" (gerund) or "cleaner" (a noun meaning a person/product that cleans, or the comparative of "clean").

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Vacillate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Hesitate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Vacillate" means to waver or keep changing one's opinion or decision; to be unable to choose between different courses of action, which is closest in meaning to "Hesitate" — to pause or be slow in acting because one is uncertain. (हिचकिचाना / झिझकना)
◦ Example: He vacillated for weeks, hesitating to accept the job offer.

• Both words describe an indecisive state of mind, whereas the other options describe decisive or forceful actions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Advance (आगे बढ़ना): To move forward or make progress — the opposite sense of indecision.

• Option 2: Stir (हिलाना): To move slightly, or to mix a liquid; can also mean to provoke, but does not carry the sense of indecision.

• Option 3: Plunge (कूद पड़ना): To jump or dive suddenly into something — suggests a decisive, sudden action, the opposite of vacillating.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Vacillate" useful for SSC: Waver, Dither, Oscillate, Fluctuate, Equivocate.

• Antonym to remember: Decide / Resolve — the opposite of vacillating is to make a firm decision.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Google on Saturday celebrated the onset of spring in the northern hemisphere with a/an ______ graphic.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. animated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes Google marking the onset of spring with a special graphic — Google's special homepage graphics (called "Doodles") are typically moving, illustrated graphics, which are correctly described as "animated" (a graphic that appears to move, made using a sequence of drawings or images).

• Contextually, "animated" is the only word among the options that logically and idiomatically pairs with "graphic" to describe a celebratory, visually engaging illustration.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "rooting" does not fit contextually — "rooting" relates to plant roots or supporting/cheering for someone, not to a type of graphic.

• Option 3: "freezing" is contextually wrong and also contradicts the idea of celebrating the onset of spring, which is associated with warmth, not freezing.

• Option 4: "implanting" means inserting something into something else (often medically or figuratively) and does not describe a type of graphic.

NOTE

• In vocabulary-based fill-in-the-blank questions, always check that the chosen word fits both the grammatical slot and the real-world context of the sentence.

• "Animated" can also describe a lively, energetic manner of speaking or behaving (e.g., "an animated discussion"), a secondary usage worth remembering for SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Reprove
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Eulogize.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Reprove" means to scold or reprimand someone, especially in a mild or gentle manner, for a fault. (डांटना / फटकारना)
◦ Example: The teacher reproved the student for arriving late.

• The opposite of scolding/criticizing is "Eulogize" — to praise someone or something highly, especially in a speech or piece of writing. (प्रशंसा करना)
◦ Example: The mayor eulogized the firefighters for their bravery.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Rap (कड़ी फटकार): To criticize or rebuke someone sharply — this is a synonym of "reprove", not its opposite.

• Option 3: Pummel (मुक्कों से मारना): To strike or hit someone repeatedly with the fists — an act of physical violence, unrelated to praise.

• Option 4: Keelhaul (कड़ी सजा देना): Originally a naval punishment of dragging someone under a ship's keel; figuratively, to reprimand someone severely — again a synonym of reprove, not an antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Reprove": Admonish, Rebuke, Chide, Reprimand, Censure.

• Other words meaning "to praise": Extol, Laud, Commend, Applaud.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Abeyance
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Continuation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Abeyance" means a state of temporary suspension or inactivity, with the expectation of resumption later. (अस्थायी निलंबन / रुकावट)
◦ Example: The project was held in abeyance until further funding was approved.

• The direct opposite of a temporary halt is "Continuation" — the act of continuing or carrying on without interruption. (निरंतरता)
◦ Example: Despite the setbacks, the continuation of the programme was ensured.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Latency (अव्यक्त अवस्था): A state of being dormant or hidden, not yet developed or active — close in meaning to abeyance, not its opposite.

• Option 2: Moratorium (रोक): An official temporary suspension of an activity, especially of a legal or financial nature — again a synonym of abeyance.

• Option 3: Layoff (छंटनी): A temporary or permanent discontinuation of employment — also conveys a stoppage, similar to abeyance rather than opposite to it.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Abeyance": Dormancy, Suspension, Recess, Hiatus.

• Other antonyms worth remembering: Persistence, Perpetuation — both convey the idea of something continuing without a break.

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
You never know when / you are going to stumble to a / jewel in the most unexpected corner.
option_2: you are going to stumble to a
option_3: jewel in the most unexpected corner.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. you are going to stumble to a.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "stumble to a". The verb "stumble", when meaning to come upon something by chance, is idiomatically followed by the prepositions "upon" or "on/across", never by "to".

• Rule — Verb-Preposition Collocation: Certain verbs take fixed prepositions with a specific meaning; "stumble upon/on/across" means to discover or encounter something accidentally, and this fixed collocation cannot be altered to "stumble to".

• Correct phrase: "...you are going to stumble upon a jewel in the most unexpected corner."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "You never know when" is grammatically correct as an introductory clause and contains no error.

• Option 3: "jewel in the most unexpected corner." is grammatically correct; the noun phrase and preposition "in" are properly used.

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist, in part 2, as explained above.

NOTE

• Other fixed verb-preposition combinations frequently tested by SSC: stumble upon/across, pounce upon, dwell on/upon, insist on, rely on, comply with, deal with.

• Do not confuse "stumble to" (incorrect) with "stumble into" (correct when meaning to enter a place clumsily or unexpectedly, e.g., "he stumbled into the room").

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.
Every of the two girls will get the reward.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Every of the two.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "Every of the two". The determiner "Every" is used only with plural countable nouns of more than two and is never followed by "of"; it must be followed directly by a singular noun (e.g., "every girl", "every student").

• Rule: For referring to two persons/things, English uses "Each of the two" or "Both of the two", and "Each" (unlike "every") can correctly be followed by "of + plural noun/pronoun".

• Correct sentence: "Each of the two girls will get the reward."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because an error clearly exists, in the phrase "Every of the two" as explained above.

• Option 2: "girls will get" is grammatically correct — the plural subject "girls" (once corrected) properly takes the plural verb "will get".

• Option 3: "the reward." is grammatically correct; the definite article and noun are properly used.

NOTE

• "Each" is used for two or more items considered individually, and can be followed by "of"; "Every" is used for three or more items considered collectively, and is never followed by "of".

• Related distinction frequently tested by SSC: "Either/neither" are used only for two, while "any/none" are used for more than two.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
He said, “I had gone to Shimla.”
option_1: He said that he had gone to Shimla.
option_2: He said that he went to Shimla.
option_3: He says that he had gone to Shimla.
option_4: He said that he has gone to Shimla.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He said that he had gone to Shimla.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct sentence "He said, 'I had gone to Shimla.'" has the reporting verb "said" in the past tense, and the reported speech is in the Past Perfect Tense ("had gone").

• Rule — Reported Speech (Tense Change): When the reporting verb is in the past tense, the Past Perfect Tense in direct speech remains unchanged as Past Perfect Tense in indirect speech (it has no further "back-shift" form, being already the most remote past tense).

• Applying the rule: the pronoun "I" changes to "he" (matching the subject), the conjunction "that" is added, and the verb "had gone" remains "had gone".
◦ Indirect: He said that he had gone to Shimla.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "went" (Simple Past) is a wrong back-shift; the Past Perfect "had gone" must remain "had gone", not change to Simple Past.

• Option 3 is incorrect because the reporting verb "says" (Present Tense) is wrong; since the original reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, it must remain "said" in indirect speech.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "has gone" (Present Perfect) is an incorrect tense; it neither matches the original Past Perfect nor follows any valid back-shift rule from "had gone".

NOTE

• Tenses that do not change when reported with a past-tense reporting verb: Past Perfect and Past Perfect Continuous, since these are already the most "back-shifted" past forms.

• General back-shift pattern: Simple Present → Simple Past; Simple Past → Past Perfect; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; Present Continuous → Past Continuous.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
At first the water ______ blue, then grey.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. seemed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence **"At first the water ______ blue, then grey" requires a linking verb that connects the subject "water" to the adjective describing its appearance ("blue"). "Seemed" is a linking verb meaning appeared to be, or gave the impression of being**, which correctly fits this context.

• Rule — Linking Verbs: Verbs like seem, appear, look, become, turn are followed directly by an adjective (not an adverb) to describe the subject's state or appearance, e.g., "The water seemed blue."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "glanced" means to take a quick look at something; it is a verb of looking performed by a person, and cannot describe the water's own appearance/colour.

• Option 3: "heeded" means to pay attention to or take notice of (advice, a warning); it cannot logically combine with a colour adjective like "blue".

• Option 4: "lest" is a conjunction meaning "for fear that" or "in order that ... not"; it is not a verb at all and cannot fill a verb slot in the sentence.

NOTE

• Common linking verbs tested by SSC: seem, appear, look, feel, taste, smell, sound, become, remain, grow, turn — all followed by an adjective, not an adverb.

• Do not confuse a linking verb ("The water seemed calm") with an action verb used with an adverb ("She looked calmly at the water").

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Ram placed her in one of the ______ leather chairs opposite his desk.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. quilted.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes "leather chairs", and the blank requires an adjective describing a type/finish of chair upholstery. "Quilted" means padded and stitched in a pattern of crossing lines, typically to hold layers of fabric/padding together, which is a common and sensible description of upholstered leather chairs.

• Contextually, "quilted leather chairs" is a natural, meaningful collocation describing furniture upholstery.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "marinated" means soaked in a seasoned liquid before cooking — this word applies to food, not furniture, and is contextually absurd here.

• Option 2: "brewed" means made by soaking/boiling/fermenting (as with tea, coffee, or beer) — again a word used for beverages, not chairs.

• Option 4: "stewed" means cooked slowly in liquid — another cooking-related word that cannot logically describe leather chairs.

NOTE

• This question type tests collocation and contextual appropriateness — always check whether the option word is semantically compatible with the noun it describes (here, "chairs" cannot be "marinated," "brewed," or "stewed," as these apply only to food/drink).

• Other adjectives that correctly describe furniture upholstery: cushioned, upholstered, padded, tufted, embossed.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Sir, can you reflect on the usefulness or __________ of blocking all the highways?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. futility.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence sets up a contrast/pairing: **"the usefulness or ______ of blocking all the highways". "Futility" means uselessness or pointlessness; the quality of having no useful result, which forms a natural antithetical pair with "usefulness"** (the two opposite possibilities being weighed).

• The construction "X or [opposite of X]" (usefulness or futility) is a common idiomatic pattern in formal English used to present two contrasting possibilities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "impotence" means a lack of power or ability (often used of physical or political powerlessness); it does not form the natural "usefulness or ___" antithetical pairing that the sentence requires.

• Option 3: "scorch" means to burn something slightly, scarring or discolouring its surface — it is unrelated in meaning to "usefulness" and does not fit grammatically as a noun of quality here.

• Option 4: "incompatibility" means the state of being unable to exist or work together — it does not pair logically with "usefulness" in this context.

NOTE

• When a sentence uses the pattern "X or Y" to weigh two possibilities, look for a word that is the direct semantic opposite of the first word given.

• Other synonyms of "futility": pointlessness, uselessness, fruitlessness, vanity (in the sense of emptiness).

question:
Select the word that is opposite in meaning (ANTONYM) to the word given below.
Sinister
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Propitious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Sinister" means giving the impression that something harmful, evil, or threatening is likely to happen. (अशुभ / अनिष्टकारी)
◦ Example: There was a sinister silence in the abandoned house.

• The opposite of something threatening or unfavourable is "Propitious" — favourable; indicating a good chance of success; auspicious. (अनुकूल / शुभ)
◦ Example: The weather was propitious for the launch of the ship.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Ominous (अशुभ): Giving the impression that something bad is going to happen — a synonym of "sinister", not its opposite.

• Option 3: Baleful (अनिष्टकर): Threatening harm; menacing — again a synonym of "sinister".

• Option 4: Foreboding (अशुभ आशंका): A feeling that something bad is going to happen — also a synonym of "sinister", describing the same sense of impending evil.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Sinister": Menacing, Malevolent, Villainous, Malign.

• Other antonyms worth remembering (words meaning favourable/auspicious): Auspicious, Favourable, Benign, Promising.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Sugest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Suggest" — meaning to put forward an idea or plan for consideration. (सुझाव देना)
◦ Example: May I suggest a different approach to this problem?

• Spelling key: SUG + GEST, with a double "g". The word "Sugest" is missing one "g".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Healthy" is correctly spelt — meaning in good physical or mental condition.

• Option 3: "Quantum" is correctly spelt — meaning a required or allowed amount, or a discrete quantity in physics.

• Option 4: "Mechanics" is correctly spelt — the branch of physics dealing with motion and forces, or the working parts/details of a system.

NOTE

• Related word family: Suggestion, Suggestive, Suggestible — all retain the double "g".

• Other frequently misspelt double-letter words in SSC exams: Occurred, Committee, Recommend, Exaggerate, Embarrass.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
Killing one’s father
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Patricide.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Patricide" means the act of killing one's own father, formed from the Latin root "pater" (father) + "-cide" (killing). (पितृहत्या)
◦ Example: The ancient tragedy centres on a king's patricide, which brings a curse upon his family.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Insecticide (कीटनाशक): A substance used for killing insects, not related to killing a father.

• Option 2: Suicide (आत्महत्या): The act of killing oneself.

• Option 3: Tyrannicide (अत्याचारी की हत्या): The killing of a tyrant or oppressive ruler.

NOTE

• Other "-cide" (killing) related one-word substitutions frequently asked by SSC: Matricide (killing one's mother), Fratricide (killing one's brother), Regicide (killing a king), Homicide (killing a person), Genocide (killing of a large group/race).

• Root to remember: Latin "caedere" meaning "to kill/cut", the source of the "-cide" suffix in all these words.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Lion’s mouth
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A dangerous situation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Lion's mouth" (often used as "to walk/venture into the lion's mouth") means to knowingly put oneself in a dangerous or perilous situation. (खतरनाक स्थिति)
◦ Example: By agreeing to testify against the gang, he was walking straight into the lion's mouth.

• The idiom draws on the image of a lion, a fierce and dangerous predator, whose mouth represents the most perilous place one could be.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Very talkative" is the meaning of a different idiom, such as "to have the gift of the gab", and is unrelated to "lion's mouth".

• Option 3: "Having no sense" would relate to idioms like "not to have an ounce of sense" or "empty-headed", not to "lion's mouth".

• Option 4: "A large share" is the meaning of the different (and commonly confused) idiom "Lion's share" — the largest part of something — which test-takers often mistake for "Lion's mouth".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Lion's mouth" (a dangerous situation) with "Lion's share" (the largest portion of something) — these are two distinct idioms frequently used as distractors for each other in SSC exams.

• Other idioms involving danger: "To play with fire", "To be on thin ice", "To beard the lion in his den" (to confront a powerful/dangerous person directly).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A bolt from the blue
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. An unexpected event.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A bolt from the blue" means a sudden and completely unexpected event, especially an unpleasant one. (अप्रत्याशित घटना)
◦ Example: The news of his resignation came as a bolt from the blue to the entire office.

• The phrase originates from the image of a bolt of lightning striking suddenly out of a clear blue sky, with no warning clouds — symbolising a shocking surprise.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "A sudden run" describes physical movement, not a surprising event, and is unrelated to the idiom's meaning.

• Option 3: "An electric shock" takes the phrase too literally — the idiom is figurative, referring to a shock of surprise, not an actual electric shock.

• Option 4: "To get hold of someone" is the meaning of a completely different idiom, unrelated to "a bolt from the blue".

NOTE

• Other idioms describing surprise/shock: "Out of the blue" (without warning, unexpectedly), "To be thunderstruck" (to be extremely surprised), "To catch someone off guard" (to surprise someone when they are unprepared).

• Note the connection between "bolt" (lightning) and "the blue" (clear sky) — both idioms "a bolt from the blue" and "out of the blue" share this imagery of the clear sky representing normalcy suddenly disrupted.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

There are so many myths about the (1) ______ impacts of milk on health. Changing how much milk you drink because of (2) ______ myths may mean you are unnecessarily restricting this (3) ______ nutritious drink. Australians often restrict dairy foods when they try to (4) ______ weight believing them to be fattening. While dairy products naturally contain fat there are many reduced fat products (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. negative.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage discusses **"myths about the ______ impacts of milk on health", and goes on to describe people "unnecessarily restricting" milk and dairy foods, believing them to be "fattening". This context of unfounded fears and unnecessary avoidance shows that the myths being discussed concern supposedly harmful/negative** impacts of milk.

• "Negative" correctly fits the context, as the entire passage is about myths that wrongly make people believe milk/dairy has bad (negative) effects on health, causing them to restrict it unnecessarily.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "kind" does not fit — "kind impacts" is not idiomatic English and does not match the passage's context of myths causing people to avoid milk.

• Option 2: "welcoming" is contextually meaningless when describing the "impacts" of a food on health.

• Option 3: "impolite" describes bad manners or rude behaviour, and cannot logically describe the "impacts" of milk on health.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the surrounding sentences fully before choosing an answer — later parts of the passage (here, "restricting... believing them to be fattening") often confirm the correct sense of an earlier blank.

• The passage's tone throughout is about correcting misconceptions, so words related to unfounded criticism or harm ("negative") fit the overall theme better than neutral or unrelated words.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

There are so many myths about the (1) ______ impacts of milk on health. Changing how much milk you drink because of (2) ______ myths may mean you are unnecessarily restricting this (3) ______ nutritious drink. Australians often restrict dairy foods when they try to (4) ______ weight believing them to be fattening. While dairy products naturally contain fat there are many reduced fat products (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. these.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a determiner that refers back to the "myths" just mentioned in the previous sentence ("myths about the negative impacts of milk on health"). "These" is the plural demonstrative determiner used to refer to something already mentioned nearby, and it correctly agrees with the plural noun "myths" that follows.

• Rule: Use "these/those" (not "this/that") before a plural noun, and use "these" rather than "those" when referring to something just mentioned in the immediately preceding sentence (near reference), as opposed to something more distant.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "those" is grammatically possible before a plural noun, but is used for reference to something more distant or already fully specified elsewhere, not for myths introduced in the immediately preceding sentence; "these" is the more natural near-reference choice here.

• Option 2: "thus" is an adverb meaning "in this way" or "therefore"; it cannot function as a determiner before the noun "myths".

• Option 4: "this" is a singular demonstrative determiner and cannot be used before the plural noun "myths" — it fails determiner-noun agreement.

NOTE

• Determiner agreement rule: this/that + singular noun; these/those + plural noun.

• This/these generally point to something nearer (in place, time, or in the preceding text); that/those point to something more distant.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

There are so many myths about the (1) ______ impacts of milk on health. Changing how much milk you drink because of (2) ______ myths may mean you are unnecessarily restricting this (3) ______ nutritious drink. Australians often restrict dairy foods when they try to (4) ______ weight believing them to be fattening. While dairy products naturally contain fat there are many reduced fat products (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. highly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the adjective "nutritious" ("restricting this ______ nutritious drink"), and requires an adverb of degree that intensifies the adjective. "Highly" is a common intensifying adverb meaning "to a great degree; very", which naturally collocates with "nutritious" (as in the common phrase "highly nutritious").

• Rule: Adverbs like "highly", "extremely", "very" are used before adjectives to intensify their meaning; "highly" specifically is the standard collocation used with words like "nutritious", "effective", "skilled", "regarded".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "suddenly" is an adverb of manner/time (meaning abruptly), not of degree, and does not logically intensify "nutritious".

• Option 2: "nominally" means "in name only, not in reality" — this would contradict the sentence's intended meaning that the drink genuinely is nutritious.

• Option 4: "invisibly" means "in a way that cannot be seen", which does not fit with describing how nutritious something is.

NOTE

• "Highly" is a fixed collocation with words such as highly nutritious, highly skilled, highly effective, highly regarded, highly unlikely.

• Do not confuse adverbs of degree (highly, extremely, very) with adverbs of manner (suddenly, invisibly) — only degree adverbs can intensify a descriptive adjective like "nutritious".

question:
Comprehension:

There are so many myths about the (1) ______ impacts of milk on health. Changing how much milk you drink because of (2) ______ myths may mean you are unnecessarily restricting this (3) ______ nutritious drink. Australians often restrict dairy foods when they try to (4) ______ weight believing them to be fattening. While dairy products naturally contain fat there are many reduced fat products (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. lose.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Australians often restrict dairy foods when they try to ______ weight believing them to be fattening." The phrase "try to lose weight" is a fixed, everyday collocation meaning to make an effort to reduce one's body weight, which fits perfectly with the context of avoiding "fattening" foods.

• Rule — Collocation: Certain verbs pair fixedly with certain nouns in English; "lose weight" (to become lighter) is the standard collocation, just as its opposite is "gain/put on weight".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "meditate" means to focus one's mind for relaxation or spiritual purposes; "meditate weight" is not a valid or meaningful collocation.

• Option 3: "subjugate" means to conquer or bring under domination/control; it does not collocate with "weight" in standard English.

• Option 4: "leverage" means to use something to maximum advantage; "leverage weight" is not an idiomatic or meaningful phrase in this context.

NOTE

• Fixed collocations with "weight" frequently tested by SSC: lose weight, gain weight, put on weight, watch one's weight, carry weight (figuratively, to have influence).

• Only "lose" correctly completes the logical cause-effect relationship in the sentence: people avoid "fattening" foods precisely because they are trying to lose (not gain) weight.

There are so many myths about the (1) ______ impacts of milk on health. Changing how much milk you drink because of (2) ______ myths may mean you are unnecessarily restricting this (3) ______ nutritious drink. Australians often restrict dairy foods when they try to (4) ______ weight believing them to be fattening. While dairy products naturally contain fat there are many reduced fat products (5) ______.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. available.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "While dairy products naturally contain fat there are many reduced fat products ______." The blank requires a word describing that such reduced-fat products exist and can be obtained/purchased, which is precisely the meaning of "available" — able to be obtained, used, or accessed.

• Contextually, the sentence is reassuring the reader that low-fat alternatives exist in the market, which "available" conveys directly and naturally.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "inoperable" means not able to be used or operated (or, medically, not treatable by surgery); it does not fit the context of dairy products being obtainable.

• Option 2: "deficient" means lacking or insufficient in some quality; this would contradict the reassuring tone of the sentence about reduced-fat products being a good option.

• Option 3: "durable" means able to withstand wear and last a long time — a term for physical toughness, irrelevant to describing perishable dairy products being obtainable.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, the final blank often summarises or resolves the point made throughout the passage — here, the passage concludes on a reassuring note that reduced-fat dairy options exist, which only "available" correctly conveys.

• Related words: accessible, obtainable, procurable — all near-synonyms of "available" often used interchangeably in reading comprehension passages.
